slides.speech: Before I say anything, look at this. On the right, that's a RickRoll. On the left, every single frame is pure random noise, and yet when it plays you can see Rick moving around in it. In about twenty minutes you'll know exactly how that works.

This is a giraffe. Turn it upside down and it's a penguin, read the label at the bottom. Nobody painted it, a model made it. On the right are cutouts with real transparency, fire, feathers, fur. Next to each one, white is solid and black is see-through. They all came from a model that only outputs plain RGB, no transparency at all. By the end of this talk you'll know how both work.

elements.text: How to Control Your (Video) Diffusion Model

slides.speech: I'm Ryan Burgert, I'm a PhD student here at Stony Brook, and this is my thesis: how to control your video diffusion model. Five papers, one question. Let me show you the question first.

slides.title: Just ask?

elements.text: The model decides everything you didn't say.

slides.speech: Say I want a cutout of a lion. So I ask for a lion isolated on a solid green background, then I key out the green. Five big models, and none of these can be keyed cleanly. Some backgrounds aren't solid, some lions turn green, one puts him in a field. That's the core problem. A prompt is a handful of words, the output is millions of pixels, so the model decides everything you didn't say, and it decides with what IT likes, not what you wanted. We'll come back to this lion in MAGICK.

slides.title: One question

elements.text: How do you control a pretrained diffusion model without building a new one?

slides.speech: So here's the one question my thesis answers: how do you get real control over a big pretrained diffusion model without building a new one? Each paper adds one handle the model never had. Sometimes the handle needs no training at all, sometimes it's a small add-on like a LoRA or a ControlNet branch, but the base model is always the one you started with. My claim is that the knowledge is already inside it. You just need the right handle to get it out.

slides.title: Diffusion, fast
slides.speech: Quick primer so the first two papers make sense. A diffusion model is trained on one job: you give it a noisy image and a prompt, here a puppy, and it predicts the noise that was added. Subtract that noise a little at a time, starting from pure static, and you get a brand new image. The snowflake means we never change its weights.

slides.title: Score Distillation

elements.text: The frozen model becomes a critic.

slides.speech: Now the trick. Instead of generating, we use the model as a critic. Take any image you want to optimize, add random noise you know, and ask the model to predict it. The difference between what it predicted and the noise you actually added tells you how to change your image so it looks more like the prompt. Then you backprop that into whatever made the image. I call it a dream loss. It means you can optimize almost anything, a mask, a print, a 3D shape, against a model you never retrain.

slides.title: Five handles
slides.speech: Here's the roadmap: five papers, five handles. Where things are, Peekaboo. What you see from each angle, Diffusion Illusions. How see-through, MAGICK. How things move, Go-with-the-Flow. And changing the motion of a video that already exists, MotionV2V. The method climbs too: the first two train nothing, then we make the training data, then we change the noise and fine-tune, then we train a control branch. Every time, the knowledge comes from the pretrained model.
Next handle: what you see from each angle. Same critic trick, but now one image has to satisfy several views at once.
Next handle: how see-through. Both of those optimize one result at a time, and Peekaboo's masks miss fine detail like hair, so this time we use the model to make training data instead.
Next handle: how things move. For video, text can't describe motion, so the handle becomes the noise itself.
Last handle: changing the motion of a video that already exists.
Those are the five handles. What I want next is one handle for any edit to any video.

slides.title: Five handles
slides.speech: So, to wrap up. Peekaboo: the model knows where things are, so you can get a mask out with no training. Diffusion Illusions: one image that reads as different pictures from different views, which won Best Demo at CVPR 2023. MAGICK: over 140,000 cutouts with real transparency, from a model that only makes RGB. Go-with-the-Flow: motion control by warping the noise, a CVPR 2025 Oral. And MotionV2V: changing the motion of a video that already exists. Other people already build on these; I co-authored three follow-ups, including Virtually Being, which uses warped noise. And Rick dancing in pure noise? The model already knew how. It just needed the right handle. Thank you, happy to take questions.
